zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset (CC BY 4.0). Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used for lexical cross-checks only; the native BnF scan governs the diplomatic text.

lines.note: Nitonito is an adverb describing the adhesion of something soft and sticky, continuing the vocabulary of the preceding page. The close printed algũacouſa is retained rather than automatically respaced.
Completes the soft, sticky description and gives nito nito suru as the example. The repetition is spaced here even though the headword Nitonito is not.
Nitten, illustrated by Nittenji, is a reverential designation for the sun. Re- continues reverencia on the next physical line.

runs.text: uerencia. Como cuſtumão os gentios, tendo que

lines.note: Completes reverencia and attributes the usage to the people the compilers call gentios. Their belief about the sun follows below; the note reports the dictionary's terminology rather than endorsing it.
Completes the reported belief that the sun is a Fotoque. The Japanese religious term is embedded in a Portuguese sentence and is visibly upright, unlike the surrounding italic words.
Nittō means going over to China, with nittō suru as the example. The second t in the repeated word is worn but agrees with the visible headword; OCR Nitiǒ misread it as i.
Niwa is a courtyard or a place for ornamental garden beds. The Portuguese alegretes is preserved rather than replaced by a modern generic word for a garden.
This separate niwa is explained by hiyori and refers to favorable or unfavorable weather. Its particular application to navigation follows below.
Nauegar completes the weather definition as conditions for sailing. The row belongs to the second Niua entry rather than the following ceremonial-fire noun.

runs.text: Fogo que ſe faz diante do Cami por

lines.note: Niwabi is a fire made before a kami for a ceremony. The initial is N, correcting OCR Miuabi; Cami is an embedded Japanese religious term, retaining its printed italic type.
Ceremonia completes the purpose of the fire. It is a genuine one-word continuation of Niuabi.

runs.text: Vaſoura com que ſe varre o pateo.

lines.note: Niwabōki is a broom for sweeping the courtyard. The headword's caron and the single visible long ſ in Vaſoura are preserved.
Niwakagoto is explained by niwakana koto, a sudden occurrence. The Portuguese re- begins repentina below.
Completes repentina, sudden. The short fragment is not a standalone definition or a missing-row artifact.
Niwakana and niwakano are alternative modifiers for something sudden. The Latin l marks the alternative and does not belong to either Japanese form.
Niwakani is labeled only as an adverb, understood with the preceding suddenness entries. No unprinted Portuguese gloss is supplied after Adu.

runs.text: Eſteira großa de palha, que ſe

lines.note: Niwamushiro is a thick straw mat. The Portuguese clause explains where it is spread on the next row, with the ß-shaped sort retained in großa.
The mat is spread in courtyards. This completes the relative clause and links the compound's niwa element to the earlier courtyard definition.

runs.text: Certo modo de caualgar no caualo

lines.note: Niwanori is a particular way of riding a horse. The setting, rather than a different animal or action, is supplied on the next row.
The riding takes place inside the courtyard. The phrase completes Niuanori without introducing a separate entry.
Niwatataki is equated with sekirei and the Portuguese bird name Arueloa, a wagtail. The historical Japanese and Portuguese spellings remain unnormalized.
Niwatazumi is standing or retained water. The following line specifies that it remains in a courtyard.
Pateo completes the definition of water left standing in the yard. Its separate physical row is retained despite containing only one word.

runs.text: Flores aßi chamadas, q̃ ſe dão

lines.note: Niwatsutsuji names flowers borne on small trees or shrubs. The visible abbreviated q̃ introduces the relative clause and is not expanded in the transcription.
The flowers grow on small trees. Aruoreſinhas corrects OCR aruoreſinlhas: the apparent extra l belongs to the h-shaped stroke sequence, not another consonant.
Niwatoko is identified as a tree or wood of that name. The mixed aſsi spelling is retained rather than made identical to nearby aßi occurrences.
Niwatori includes both hen and cock. The two Portuguese nouns make the non-sex-specific scope of the Japanese headword explicit.

runs.text: Certa laya de cereijeiras pequenas q̃

lines.note: Niwazakura denotes a kind of small cherry tree. Enlargement supports cereijeiras, with the weak r and the additional e missed by OCR cerijeiras; this historical spelling is not replaced with modern cerejeiras.
The small trees are planted in gardens or courtyards. Niuas is the Japanese garden term used with a Portuguese plural ending inside an otherwise Portuguese sentence.
Niuma is a packhorse; the example begins loading goods onto it. The printed Nivmani preserves the internal v allograph rather than being silently changed to u.
The verb completes the packhorse example, glossed as loading the horse. Its initial v and circumflex are preserved in vôſuru rather than normalized to a modern spelling.

runs.text: Duas figuras grandes como gigantes, ou

lines.note: Niō denotes two large guardian figures, compared with giants. The long vowel has a caron; the objects and their location are further specified below.

runs.text: eſtatuas que ſe poem nas portas das varelas.

lines.note: The figures are statues placed at temple gates. Varelas is retained as the Portuguese term used here, without replacing it with a modern Japanese building name.
Nio is described as a sea duck of that name. The final i of aßi corrects OCR aßa; domar retains the source's close spacing, and no precise modern bird species is imposed.
Nioi is the noun for smell or fragrance. It is a separate entry from the inflected verb that follows.
The niou verb is glossed as giving off a smell. The example begins with flowers in various forms or colors, and the two circumflexes in the principal parts remain distinct from nearby carons.

The concessive niwoyedomo describes the flowers' fragrance, followed by the absence of a master on whom to depend. The source's fitomonǒ spelling and attached particles are retained rather than respaced or modernized.

runs.text: Lib. 4. Posto que as roſas chei-

lines.note: Feiq. is the upright source label, followed by an italic book reference and the translation. The scan has chei-, beginning cheirão, not OCR chet-; Posto retains the baseline s/t classification.

runs.text: rão, toda via não tendo dono nem ſenhor, a que

lines.note: Completes cheirão and says the flowers have neither owner nor lord. The printed toda via remains two words, and the relative clause continues below.
Completes the absence of a patron to whom the flowers can entrust themselves. This closes the cited illustration of niuoi rather than adding another verb sense.

runs.text: Tecidura de armas de fio verme-

lines.note: Nioikata names an armor-lacing arrangement. The Portuguese begins the color specification with verme-, continued as vermelho below.
Completes vermelho and specifies a red thread between two white ones. The color arrangement, not an odor, explains this use of the nioi-related term.

Nioiuma is equated with konida and glossed as a packhorse. The final a is heavily abraded but retains its right-hand stroke without an i dot; enlargement and the supplied NINJAL entry support Niuoivma over OCR Niuoivmi.

runs.text: Dous mundos. i, Eſte preſente, & o

lines.note: Nise here means two worlds or lives, namely the present and the future. Dous corrects OCR Dour, and the explanatory i remains part of the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Futuro supplies the second of the two worlds, completing the definition. It is a separate physical row, not a page catchword.
Niseru means making something resemble another, imitating, or counterfeiting it. The printed single long ſ in Aſemelhar and abbreviated cõ- are preserved.
Completes contrafazer and introduces imitating another person's handwriting. Ar- continues as Arremedar at the top of column 2, so the text must not be treated as a page-ending catchword.

runs.text: remedar, ou imitar a letra dalguem. ¶

lines.note: This continues Ar-/remedar from the preceding column: copying or imitating another person's handwriting. The roman Fi- begins the next Japanese example, not a separate entry.

Fitono cataguiuo niſuru means imitating someone's character or habits. The worn u after t in custumes is retained from its surviving lower stroke; the OCR had dropped it, while the historical u spelling is not modernized.
This completes the Portuguese explanation, 'of someone'; it belongs to the example above and has no independent headword.
Nixecoto denotes a fabricated or counterfeit thing. The scan has the continuous word contrafeita, not the OCR's broken and malformed cos tra feita.
The example means saying invented things; yǔ retains the marked vowel of the printed verb. The hyphen divides Portuguese fingi-/das across the physical lines.

runs.text: das, ou contrafeitas pera enganar a alguem.

lines.note: The invented or counterfeit statements are made to deceive someone. The final a alguem is preserved rather than regularized away.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe aſemelha, ou he tira-

lines.note: Nixemono is described as something resembling or copied from another thing. The single long s in aſemelha and the physical tira- ending are retained.
This completes tira-/da por outra, 'copied after another'; it is a continuation of the imitation entry.
Nixeſoconai is failure to imitate successfully; the inflectional forms carry carons, not circumflexes. The Portuguese clause continues with its object below.
The example describes failing in the imitation on both sides. The line-final muſ- joins ſato on the next line, so neither long s is discarded.
The Japanese concludes with a judgment about the person, followed by the upright citation Mon. Portuguese Errã- begins the explanation using a nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: do em imitar ambas as partes. i, Nem imi-

lines.note: The gloss explains the failure to imitate either side adequately. The scan's explanatory i, ends in a comma, correcting the OCR period; imi- continues the following nasalized verb.

runs.text: tãdo bem hũ nẽ outro, he homẽ pera pouco, ou

lines.note: Neither one nor the other is imitated well, and the person is described as of little ability. The marks belong to nẽ and homẽ, not the OCR grave-accented nè and malformed homò.
De pouco tomo supplies a second expression for little standing or worth, completing the preceding assessment rather than naming another object.
This Nixi is the direction west, defined by Portuguese Poente; it is distinct from the shellfish homograph below.

runs.text: Certo genero de mariſco, como buzeos.

lines.note: The second Nixi is a kind of shellfish compared with whelk-like shells. The general comparison does not establish a modern species, and buzeos is kept as printed.
Nixigara means the shell of that shellfish; deste explicitly links the definition to the preceding homograph.
Niximuqi means facing or toward the west. The initial is visibly N, correcting Xiximuqi; the close printed partedo is retained, and Ni- starts the example across the line break.
The full example Niximuqini nauoru means turning or changing orientation westward. The historical nauoru form is retained rather than modernized.
This completes the direction of the turn: toward the west. Occidente is the Portuguese counterpart of Nixi in this entry.
Nixin, paraphrased as Futavoya, means the two parents, father and mother. Both Japanese expressions are upright entry material, not font-toggle terms embedded in Portuguese.
Here Nixin is a double or divided heart, with Futagocoro as its Japanese synonym. The Portuguese describes a false or treacherous heart; refalſado is retained literally.
Atreiçoado completes the alternative description 'treacherous.' Its historical initial a and spelling are not replaced with a modern form.

runs.text: Nome de hum peixe do mar.

lines.note: This third Nixin is the name of a sea fish. The printed definition gives no further identifying details, so the note does not insert a species into the text.
This Nixiqi is the faculty or sense of hearing, distinct from the textile homograph. The final register label S. is upright, outside the italic Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Certa laya de peças como brocadilho.

lines.note: The second Nixiqi refers to a kind of fabric compared with brocade. The historical laya and brocadilho are preserved, with no added textile classification.

runs.text: P. Pao pintado que ſe punha à

lines.note: Nixiqigui is painted wood used in a former courting custom. The introductory P. is printed in the italic explanatory run; the final à leads into the placement below.

runs.text: porta antigamente da molher que hum pretẽdia.

lines.note: The painted wood was placed at the door of the woman being courted. The abbreviation mark in pretẽdia is on e and remains unexpanded.
Nixǒ is glossed as two generations. The caron in the Japanese and the tilde on e in geraçoẽs are distinct marks and are preserved.

runs.text: Certa ceremonia que fazem os Ienxùs

lines.note: Nixxit names a ceremony performed by the Ienxùs. Ienxùs is a Japanese religious designation within Portuguese and remains italic as printed; its grave accent is retained.
The ceremony occurs in religious services or funeral observances. Officios and ſaimentos complete the definition without introducing a further Japanese example.
Nixxocu means a solar eclipse. The visible cl sequence gives Eclypſe, correcting OCR Echypſe; the roman ſu- begins the verb ſuru across the break.
This completes Nixxocu ſuru, for the sun to be eclipsed. The gloss repeats the historical Eclypſ- spelling found in the preceding line.
Nixxoſa is paraphrased as everyday actions or work. Mainichino xoſa is the upright Japanese synonym, and ca- belongs to Portuguese ca-/da.
The short continuation completes 'of each day,' closing the definition of daily actions.
Nixxu is the number of days, with Ficazu as its Japanese equivalent. The repeated Nixxu- begins an example that continues with the object particle on the next line.

The example means specifying or setting particular days. Although sadamuru would be the expected verb, the enlarged scan shows a right-projecting crossbar in fadamuru unlike the nearby ſaſu; the printed f is therefore retained as an anomaly, not silently changed to ſ.

runs.text: Hũa laya de nacida, ou in-

lines.note: This names a kind of boil or swelling. Hũa keeps its nasal abbreviation, and in- begins the word for swelling across the physical line break.
The historical definition describes the swelling as small but very dangerous. This completes in-/chaço and does not warrant identifying a modern diagnosis.
Niyaxi is the transitive act of making something boil or cooking it over a fire. The principal part aita is the historical form printed here, not a missing modern ending.
After the literal cooking sense, Per met. introduces the figurative Xinyuo niyaſu, becoming angry. The Portuguese label is uniformly italic; Xinyuo and niyaſu are upright example text.
This completes En-/colorizarſe, the anger gloss. The printed o in colorizarſe is retained instead of silently normalizing the word to a modern spelling.
Niye gives the corresponding intransitive cooking or boiling verb. Itẽ introduces an additional sense below, and its tilde is retained.
The further sense is boiling audibly. The example begins 'this kettle boils well'; the circumflex in yô and the physical ni- ending are preserved.

runs.text: Esta panela do Chanoyu coze, l, faz

lines.note: This completes ni-/yuru and describes a tea-ceremony kettle that boils water well. The scan's tall initial C gives Chanoyu; the embedded Japanese term remains italic with the Portuguese sentence.
The clause completes the alternate wording, 'makes the water boil well.' Agoa is the historical printed spelling, not modern água.
Niyedono is defined as a kitchen. It is the final body entry; the separate Niye- below is the catchword for the following page, not part of this definition.
